steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.

builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Rational Use of Time for Social Coordination in Humans and AI
summary: The study replaces explicit-communication coordination protocols with a benchmark (The Mind card game) in which agents must coordinate using only pause timing, comparing 150 humans against computer-use agents and text-prompted LLMs under a Bayesian model of partner-belief inference. It costs nothing to deploy directly, but operationalizing continuous-time cues in production agents adds interface complexity (timestamp capture, latency-sensitive turn handling) that standard text-prompted LLM pipelines do not natively support. The key failure mode is precisely what the paper documents: models can represent a Bayesian-style timing strategy yet fail to adapt to a specific partner across repeated interactions, so systems built on implicit temporal signaling may coordinate poorly in long-horizon or repeated-interaction deployments.
rationale: This is an evaluation study of multi-agent coordination via implicit timing signals rather than a deployable technique, so it informs how the reader should assess interactive agents but offers no component to adopt on constrained infrastructure.
technique: Temporal-cue social coordination benchmark for AI agents

claims.statement: The study replaces explicit-communication coordination protocols with a benchmark (The Mind card game) in which agents must coordinate using only pause timing, comparing 150 humans against computer-use agents and text-prompted LLMs under a Bayesian model of partner-belief inference. It costs nothing to deploy directly, but operationalizing continuous-time cues in production agents adds interface complexity (timestamp capture, latency-sensitive turn handling) that standard text-prompted LLM pipelines do not natively support. The key failure mode is precisely what the paper documents: models can represent a Bayesian-style timing strategy yet fail to adapt to a specific partner across repeated interactions, so systems built on implicit temporal signaling may coordinate poorly in long-horizon or repeated-interaction deployments.

Frontier models' timing behavior in a cooperative card game is best captured by a Bayesian partner-belief inference strategy, similar to humans, but unlike humans none of the tested models efficiently adapt their behavior to partners over the course of the game.
